**The Return**

The book came back on a Tuesday, which the librarian would later think was the right day for it. Tuesdays have no ceremony. Nobody expects anything of a Tuesday.

The man who brought it was perhaps seventy, wearing a coat too heavy for October. He set it on the counter the way you set down something you've carried a long time and no longer trust your hands with. A hardback. Green cloth, faded to the color of pond water at the spine. *Field Guide to the Birds of Eastern North America*, 1966 edition.

"I'd like to return this," he said.

She turned it over. The pocket inside the back cover still had the card in it. The last stamp read APR 12 1983.

"That's—" she began.

"Forty-one years," he said. "I did the arithmetic in the parking lot."

She almost laughed, then didn't. He wasn't smiling. He wasn't not smiling either. He had the face of someone standing at the edge of a story, deciding whether to step in.

"There's no fine," she said. "We stopped charging fines in 2019. And anyway this would have been"—she did her own arithmetic—"a lot. We'd have just replaced it and moved on."

"I know. I looked it up. I wasn't worried about the fine."

He stayed at the counter. Behind him a woman with two toddlers was trying to find a picture book about excavators, and the toddlers were narrating their own search at volume. The man didn't seem to hear them.

"I checked it out for my brother," he said. "He was eleven. I was fourteen. He'd gotten interested in birds that spring, and we didn't have anything at the house, and I had the library card. He didn't have his own yet. He kept it by his bed. Had a notebook where he wrote down everything he saw. Chickadee. Chickadee. Chickadee. Cardinal, female. He got very excited about the female cardinal because it wasn't red and he'd figured it out anyway."

The librarian understood, from the shape of the telling, where this was going, and let it go there.

"He died that June. Swimming. It's a long way from here and it doesn't matter. I put the book in a box with his notebook and some other things, and my mother put the box in the attic, and then my mother died and the house was sold and the box came to me, and I've moved four times with it and never opened it until last month."

"Why last month?"

He thought about that. Behind him one of the toddlers had found the excavator book and was announcing it.

"My granddaughter asked me what kind of bird was in the yard. I didn't know. I said, I used to have a book. And then I couldn't sleep, so I went and got the box."

He opened the guide and turned it toward her. The pages were soft, the way old paper gets, and someone had pencilled small checkmarks in the margins. Not many. Eleven, maybe twelve. Chickadee. Cardinal. Blue jay. Downy woodpecker. A checkmark beside the mourning dove that was darker than the others, pressed hard, as though the boy had been especially sure.

"He only got to the ones you can see from a kitchen window," the man said. "He was going to do the warblers in the fall. He'd read ahead."

She turned the page. A brown thrasher, unchecked.

"I don't want the book," he said. "That's not why I'm here. I mean—I don't need to keep it. I've had it forty-one years and I looked at it for the first time last month. It's not mine. It never was. It was his for about ten weeks and it was yours the rest of the time. I just thought it ought to come back."

She should have said something about deaccessioning, about how a 1966 field guide had no place in the current collection, about how it would go in the donation bin and probably sell for a dollar at the Friends of the Library sale in March. Someone would buy it for the illustrations and cut them out for a craft project. That was the honest end of most returned books that had been gone this long.

Instead she said, "Do you want a minute with it before I take it?"

He shook his head. Then he put one finger on the mourning dove, the heavy checkmark, and held it there for about as long as it takes to say a name. Then he took his hand back.

"He was right about that one," he said. "I heard one this morning. I'd forgotten I knew the sound."

He left. He didn't take a new card. He didn't look at anything else. The door swung shut behind him and the mother with the toddlers came up to check out the excavator book and the librarian scanned it and said the due date and smiled at the child, who was not listening.

Then she picked up the green book and did not put it in the donation bin.

There is a shelf in the back office where librarians keep things that don't fit. Local pamphlets nobody has catalogued. A yearbook someone left. A hand-drawn map of the town from 1950 with a note that says *don't throw this away*. She put the field guide there, between the map and the yearbook, and she wrote on a slip of paper *returned 41 years late, do not discard*, and did not sign it, because she didn't think it needed a name. It had a name already. Two of them, if you counted the checkmarks.

She went back to the desk. Outside, it had started to rain, a thin October rain that made the parking lot shine. She thought about the man driving home in it. She thought about a boy at a kitchen window in 1983 with a pencil, sure about a dove.

Some things stay checked out. That's the whole of it. The card in the back says one date and the world says another, and the difference is not a fine. It's just the time it takes.
